articles.title: Did China use a 'honeypot' to influence Nvidia CEO? US Congress wants answers
articles.summary: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang is facing growing pressure as US lawmakers raise concerns over whether his relationship with a woman suspected of having links to
articles.body: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang is facing growing pressure as US lawmakers raise concerns over whether his relationship with a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence could have compromised American national security.On Wednesday, Congressman Jamie Raskin said Congress was more concerned about the possible impact of the alleged relationship on US national security than Huang's position as the head of the chipmaker."The fate of Mr Huang as the CEO of his companies is up to his board. Apparently, he exercises a lot of influence over his board," Raskin said, adding that the decision to retain or remove him was a matter for the company's directors.However, he said lawmakers had a legitimate reason to examine whether China had used an alleged "honeypot scheme" to influence a major American corporate executive.Raskin alleged that the woman, suspected of acting on behalf of China, may have influenced Huang, who in turn used his financial influence to persuade President Donald Trump to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to China."Did this whole scheme end up compromising the national security of the United States? That is our legitimate interest," he said, adding that Congress was likely to hold oversight hearings on the matter.Earlier, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticised Trump for allegedly failing to act despite being briefed more than a year ago about Huang's reported relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.Schumer said the reports raised serious questions about the administration's handling of national security concerns involving one of America's most important technology companies."Trump has been busy trying to defend Jensen Huang, when he ought to be defending our national security," Schumer said.He also called on Congress to pass bipartisan legislation, including the AI Oversight Act, the MATCH Act and the Chip Security Act, to restrict China's access to advanced American technology.Nvidia board weighs Jensen Huang's futureMeanwhile, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board of directors was preparing to remove Huang as CEO, citing people familiar with the matter. The reported move follows allegations about his relationship with a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.Huang has acknowledged the alleged affair and reportedly discussed his infidelity with employees during meetings on Monday and Tuesday.Following his acknowledgement, Nvidia's board said it had launched an investigation into the matter. The probe is being led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.The New York Times separately reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him.According to the NYT, Huang and Powell, 48, were captured on video behaving affectionately at a hotel in San Jose, California, during an Nvidia conference in March.Suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang in BeijingAdding to the row, Megaspeed International founder Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy at the centre of the scandal, is currently living in Beijing.Security officials are aware of her presence in the Chinese capital, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.A CBS News reporter also said in a post on X that Nvidia's board was preparing to discuss Jensen Huang's future, with the Trump administration aware of plans to remove him from the position.The controversy has also weighed on Nvidia's shares. CBS reported that the company's stock fell more than 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday following The Wall Street Journal's report, extending a multi-day decline.Nvidia was co-founded by Jensen Huang in 1993. The company designs some of the world's most powerful semiconductors, which are widely used by leading artificial intelligence firms. Its advanced chips are considered strategically important, with US export controls restricting their sale to China.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Roberto Clemente's three sons sought $45 million after Puerto Rico put the baseball legend's image on commemorative plates; the US Supreme Court refused their appeal on November 9, leaving other claims unresolved
articles.summary: A sporting legend's legacy can live far beyond the stadium, but deciding who controls that legacy can become a complicated legal battle.
articles.body: A sporting legend's legacy can live far beyond the stadium, but deciding who controls that legacy can become a complicated legal battle. More than half a century after Roberto Clemente's death, his name and image have become the subject of a dispute between his family and his native Puerto Rico. In 2022, the US territory issued souvenir license plates featuring the baseball star without his sons' consent, causing a dispute. Now, the US Supreme Court's refusal to hear their appeal has left the family's fight over trademark rights and compensation unresolved.Supreme Court declines to interveneAccording to Reuters and ESPN, the Supreme Court declined on November 9 to consider an appeal filed by Clemente's three sons against Puerto Rico's use of their father's likeness on commemorative licence plates and vehicle registration tags.Roberto Clemente Jr, Luis Roberto Clemente and Roberto Enrique Clemente had challenged the programme, arguing that the government had appropriated trademark rights belonging to the family. Their lawsuit, filed alongside two companies they own that work to protect Clemente's brand and philanthropic legacy, sought to prevent future use of his image on vehicle plates.The family also sought $45 million in damages and an additional $3.15 million in compensation for trademark infringement. The sons maintained that the programme generated approximately $15 million for Puerto Rico through the sale of the commemorative registrations.The Supreme Court rejected the appeal without providing an explanation. However, the decision does not resolve every aspect of the wider dispute. According to Reuters, the family's legal representatives intend to continue pursuing the claims that remain before the lower courts.How the commemorative plates sparked a disputePuerto Rico introduced the special plates and registration tags in 2022 to mark the 50th anniversary of Clemente's death. The designs featured his portrait, his iconic Pittsburgh Pirates jersey number 21 and recognition of his remarkable achievement of recording 3,000 career hits.According to USA Today, the registration programme involved fees of $21 and $5, which collectively generated around $15 million for the territory. The initiative was introduced during a difficult economic period, as Puerto Rico continued recovering from bankruptcy.Clemente's children objected to the arrangement because the revenue went to the government rather than businesses associated with preserving and promoting their father's legacy. The programme was discontinued at the end of 2022.The family subsequently filed a lawsuit, arguing that the unauthorised commercial use of Clemente's identity amounted to a government taking of private property under the Fifth Amendment of the US Constitution.Trademark rights at the centre of the legal battleThe central question concerned whether constitutional protections against government seizure of private property extend automatically to intangible assets such as trademarks.A federal district court in San Juan, presided over by Judge Gina Méndez-Miró, dismissed the family's case. The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals subsequently upheld parts of that decision, rejecting the argument that Puerto Rico's use of the trademarks constituted an unconstitutional taking.According to Reuters and ESPN, the family's lawyers argued before the Supreme Court that the lower courts had weakened constitutional safeguards by treating trademark rights differently from physical property.Puerto Rico claimed the appeals court can protect intangible property under the Constitution. Its legal representatives argued that the decision simply applied existing Supreme Court precedents to the circumstances of the case.Remembering a baseball iconThe dispute concerns the legacy of one of baseball's most celebrated players. Born in Carolina, Puerto Rico, Clemente spent 18 seasons with the Pittsburgh Pirates between 1955 and 1972.He earned 15 All-Star selections, won two World Series championships and finished his career with exactly 3,000 hits, alongside a .317 batting average, according to USA Today. He was inducted posthumously into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1973.Clemente died on December 31, 1972, aged 38, when the aircraft carrying him humanitarian supplies to earthquake victims in Nicaragua crashed.His sporting achievements and humanitarian contributions have made his identity an enduring part of baseball history. His sons' remaining legal claims mean the dispute over who controls and profits from Clemente's image may continue after the Supreme Court's Nov. 9 decision.Images Courtesy: istock and Roberto Clemente websiteYou use AI every day.
